1.note: Zechariah is using the words translated as **The burden of the word of Yahweh** to introduce a new section of his prophecy. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
The word translated as **in** could mean: (1) concerning. Alternate translation: [about the land of] (2) against. Alternate translation: [against the land of]
The pronoun **his** could refer to: (1) Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s resting place] or (2) the word of Yahweh. Alternate translation: [the resting place of Yahweh’s word]

1.q: כִּ֤י לַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ עֵ֣ין אָדָ֔ם וְ⁠כֹ֖ל שִׁבְטֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
1.note: This could mean: (1) Yahweh is attentive to all the world and especially Israel. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s eyes watch all of mankind and all of the tribes of Israel] or (2) everyone in the world, including Israel, are attentive to Yahweh. Alternate translation: [all of mankind and all of the tribes of Israel watch Yahweh]

2.note: The pronoun **it** refers to the land of Hadrach and Damascus. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [borders on the land of Hadrach and Damascus]

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [as do Tyre and Sidon]

Here, **they** represents the people who live in **Tyre and Sidon**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Tyre and Sidon, for their inhabitants are very wise]

Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for they consider themselves very wise]

3.note: Zechariah is speaking of the city **Tyre** as if it were a living woman who **built herself a stronghold**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the people of Tyre have built themselves a stronghold]

The word **herself** indicates that the object of the verb is the same as the subject of the verb. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate that the same person fills two roles in the sentence. Alternate translation: [And Tyre has built a stronghold for her own benefit]

The point of this comparison is that just as **dust** and **the mud of the streets** are extremely common and plentiful, so the **silver** and **refined gold** that Tyre accumulated were extremely abundant. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [heaped up silver and refined gold in very great abundance]

4.note: Behold! The Lord is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]
The pronoun **her** refers to the city of Tyre. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The Lord will dispossess Tyre]

4.q: וְ⁠הִכָּ֥ה בַ⁠יָּ֖ם חֵילָ֑⁠הּ וְ⁠הִ֖יא בָּ⁠אֵ֥שׁ תֵּאָכֵֽל
4.note: Zechariah is speaking of the city of Tyre as if it were a living woman whose wealth could be struck **down** and who would be **devoured by fire**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will destroy the wealth of that city on the sea, and the city will be destroyed by fire]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wealth**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [strike down all she owns]

Here, fire represents “destruction in war.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and she will be destroyed in war]

Zechariah is stating the pronoun **she** separately, even though the verb translated as **will be devoured** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Tyre itself will be destroyed. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Tyre itself will be devoured by fire]

The expression she will be devoured by fire is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and fire will devour her]

5.note: Here, **Ashkelon**, **Gaza**, and **Ekron** represent the people who live in those cities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Ashkelon … and the people of Gaza … And the people of Ekron]

Here Zechariah is speaking as if Gaza’s terror were a physical pain that would make the city **writhe greatly**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Gaza also will be greatly distressed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **hope**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for she no longer expects good things to happen]

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And Ekron will also see and tremble, for her hope has dried up]

Here Zechariah is speaking of Ekron’s **hope** as if it were a stream or spring that has **dried up**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [she has no more hope]

The expression **Ashkelon will not be inhabited** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people will no longer inhabit Ashkelon]

6.note: The pronoun **I** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh will cut off the pride]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the **pride of the Philistines** were something that he could **cut off** with a blade. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I will put an end to the arrogance of the Philistines]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pride**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the Philistines are proud of]

Here, **the pride of the Philistines** represents their mightiness as seen in the glory of their king and their controlling who lives in their own cities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I will make the Philistines an insignificant people group]

7.q: וַ⁠הֲסִרֹתִ֨י דָמָ֜י⁠ו מִ⁠פִּ֗י⁠ו וְ⁠שִׁקֻּצָי⁠ו֙ מִ⁠בֵּ֣ין שִׁנָּ֔י⁠ו
7.note: Here, **his blood** and **his abominations** represent the meat with blood in it and the food sacrificed to idols that the Philistines ate. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And I will remove the meat with blood in it from his mouth and the food sacrificed to idols from between his teeth]

7.q: וַ⁠הֲסִרֹתִ֨י דָמָ֜י⁠ו מִ⁠פִּ֗י⁠ו וְ⁠שִׁקֻּצָי⁠ו֙ מִ⁠בֵּ֣ין שִׁנָּ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠נִשְׁאַ֥ר גַּם־ה֖וּא לֵֽ⁠אלֹהֵ֑י⁠נוּ וְ⁠הָיָה֙ כְּ⁠אַלֻּ֣ף בִּֽ⁠יהוּדָ֔ה
7.note: The pronouns **his** and **he** both refer to the Philistines. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I will remove the Philistines’ blood from their mouth and their abominations from between their teeth, and they also will be left behind for our God, and they will be like a clan in Judah]

The point of these comparisons is that just as a clan in Judah belongs fully to Yahweh’s people, so the surviving Philistines will belong to Yahweh’s people, and just as a Jebusite was absorbed into Israel, so Ekron will be absorbed among them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and the surviving Philistines will belong to Yahweh’s people just as a clan in Judah does, and the people of Ekron will be absorbed among them just as the Jebusites were]

8.q: וְ⁠חָנִ֨יתִי לְ⁠בֵיתִ֤⁠י מִצָּבָה֙ מֵ⁠עֹבֵ֣ר וּ⁠מִ⁠שָּׁ֔ב וְ⁠לֹֽא־יַעֲבֹ֧ר עֲלֵי⁠הֶ֛ם ע֖וֹד נֹגֵ֑שׂ כִּ֥י עַתָּ֖ה רָאִ֥יתִי בְ⁠עֵינָֽ⁠י
8.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the last phrase gives the reason for the result that the rest of the verse describes. Alternate translation: [I am paying close attention to what happens to my people like one camping around my house as a guard against the one passing through and against the one returning, and no oppressor will pass over them again.]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if he were an army that would **camp around** his **house** to protect it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will stand guard around my house]

Here, **my house** represents his temple and the people connected with it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [my temple and those who belong to it]

Yahweh is using the expressions **the one passing through** and **the one returning** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use such expressions in the same way. If not, you can translate them with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [against enemies who pass through and the enemies who return]
The pronoun **them** refers to the people connected with Yahweh’s house. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [my people]

Here, **now I have seen with my eyes** represents “I have begun to pay close attention to and care for my people.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [now I have begun to care for my people]

9.q: גִּילִ֨י מְאֹ֜ד בַּת־צִיּ֗וֹן הָרִ֨יעִי֙ בַּ֣ת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם
9.note: The two clauses **Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion** and **Shout, daughter of Jerusalem** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Rejoice with great joy, people of Zion and Jerusalem!]

The expression **being saved** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God saves him]

Here Zechariah is speaking of the people of Jerusalem as if they were a **daughter of Zion** or **daughter of Jerusalem**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people of Zion … people of Jerusalem]

Zechariah is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. There are not two donkeys. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them. Alternate translation: [and riding on a donkey, even on a young donkey] or [and riding on a donkey’s colt]

It might seem that the expression **a colt, the son of female donkeys** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [a young donkey]

10.note: The pronoun **I** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh will cut off the chariot from Ephraim]

10.q: וְ⁠הִכְרַתִּי־רֶ֣כֶב מֵ⁠אֶפְרַ֗יִם וְ⁠סוּס֙ מִ⁠יר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם וְ⁠נִכְרְתָה֙ קֶ֣שֶׁת מִלְחָמָ֔ה
10.note: Here, **the chariot from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem, and the bow of war** represents the military power of those regions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will remove all the military power from Ephraim and from Jerusalem]

The expression **the bow of war will be cut off** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will cut off the bow of war]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **bow** that is characterized by its use in **war**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the bow used in war]

Zechariah is using **speak peace** as a common expression of the culture to mean “proclaim peace.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he will make peace with the nations] or [And he will make the nations behave peacefully]
The pronoun **he** refers to the king mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the king will speak peace to the nations]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **dominion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he will rule from sea to sea]

Yahweh is referring to all of the earth by naming two major regions, **from sea to sea, and from the River to the ends of the earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [across the entire earth]

11.note: Here Zechariah is using the phrase **As for you also** to introduce the people of Jerusalem as the ones Yahweh now addresses directly. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [As for you also, O Jerusalem]

Here, **the blood of your covenant** represents the sacrificial blood by which Yahweh confirmed his covenant with the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [by the sacrificial blood that sealed my covenant with you]
The pronoun **I** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh has set free your prisoners]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the exile and suffering of the people as if they were **prisoners** held in a **pit in which there is no water**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your captives who are dying in desperate misery]

12.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **hope**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [prisoners who are hopeful]

Here Yahweh is speaking of a place of safety and security as if it were a **stronghold** to which the people could return. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Return to the place where you will be safe, prisoners of hope]

Yahweh is using **return double to you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “restore to you twice as much as you have lost.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that I will restore to you twice as much as you have lost]

13.note: Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [in that]

Yahweh is using **your sons, Zion** and **your sons, Greece** as common expressions of the culture to mean the people of Zion and the people of Greece. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Zion against the people of Greece]

13.q: דָרַ֨כְתִּי לִ֜⁠י יְהוּדָ֗ה קֶ֚שֶׁת מִלֵּ֣אתִי אֶפְרַ֔יִם
13.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the people of **Judah** as if they were a **bow** that he bends and of **Ephraim** as the arrow that he uses. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have made the people of Judah like a bow for myself, and I have made the people of Ephraim like arrows]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I have filled Ephraim as a quiver of arrows]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the sword of a mighty man** is powerful and effective in battle, so Yahweh will make his people powerful against their enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and I will make you very powerful in battle]

14.note: The pronoun **them** refers to Yahweh’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh will appear over his people]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the lightning** flashes suddenly and strikes powerfully, so Yahweh’s **arrow** will strike his enemies swiftly and powerfully. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and his arrow will go out suddenly and strike powerfully]

14.q: וַֽ⁠אדֹנָ֤⁠י יְהֹוִה֙ בַּ⁠שּׁוֹפָ֣ר יִתְקָ֔ע וְ⁠הָלַ֖ךְ בְּ⁠סַעֲר֥וֹת תֵּימָֽן
14.note: Zechariah is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a warrior. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the Lord Yahweh will blow on the trumpet and advance furiously, like a mighty warrior]

15.note: The pronoun **them** refers to Yahweh’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh of Armies will defend his people]

Here Zechariah is speaking of the people utterly defeating their enemies as if they would **devour** them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will completely defeat and will subdue those who attack them]

The point of this comparison is that just as men who have drunk **wine** become loud and boisterous, so the people will **drink and roar** in their triumph. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they will drink and roar in triumph just as drunk men roar]

The point of this comparison is that just as the bowl and the corners of the altar were filled with sacrificial blood, so the people will be full. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and they will be as full as the bowl and the corners of the altar are filled with sacrificial blood]

16.note: The pronouns **their** and **them** refer to Yahweh’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh the God of his people will save his people]

Zechariah is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See the Introduction to Zechariah for a discussion of the phrase “in that day.”
The pronoun **they** refers to Yahweh’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [for his people are the stones of a crown]

The point of this comparison is that just as a shepherd rescues and protects the flock of his people, so Yahweh will save and care for his people on that day. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as a shepherd saves his sheep]

Here the word **for** introduces not a reason but an expansion. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [indeed to him]

Here Zechariah is speaking of Yahweh’s people as if they were **the stones of a crown** that sparkle beautifully. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they are precious to him and glorious over his land]

17.note: Zechariah is using phrases that express a strong feeling of admiration and praise. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Everything is amazing and wonderful]

The pronoun **his** could refer to: (1) the people. Alternate translation: [how good and beautiful every one is] or (2) Yahweh. Alternate translation: [how great is Yahweh’s goodness, and how great is Yahweh’s beauty] It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **goodness** and **beauty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [how good he is, and how beautiful]

Zechariah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Grain will make the young men flourish, and new wine will make the virgins flourish]
